name: Egersund
title: Egersund Hull Gauging | Pelagic Vessels and Module Barges
description: Thickness gauging in Egersund for pelagic fishing vessels, reefers, heavy-lift ships and transport barges: RSW tanks, hull plating and deck structure.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Fishing Vessels and Barges in Egersund
intro: Egersund is one of Norway's most important fishing harbours, where large pelagic vessels land herring, mackerel, horse mackerel and blue whiting for freezing ashore. The same sheltered harbour serves an offshore fabrication yard whose modules leave on barges and heavy-lift ships. Fishing vessels between seasons, reefers loading frozen fish and barges awaiting load-out all spend time at the quays, which is when their steel can be measured. Each job is carried out by technicians who fly in from India for that vessel.

highlights.p: Pelagic vessels keep their catch in refrigerated sea-water tanks, where chilled circulating seawater, fish residues and frequent washing attack the steel. Gauging tank plating, bulkheads and internal stiffeners while the vessel lies between seasons shows where coating breakdown has turned into real metal loss.

Modules built at the fabrication yard sail out on transport barges and heavy-lift ships. Measuring barge deck plating, internal framing and ballast tanks before loading gives the barge owner documented condition to put in front of the voyage planners and the marine warranty surveyor.

highlights.h: Almost no tide to plan around
highlights.p: Egersund sits near an amphidromic point, so the tidal range is practically nil. Quay heights hardly change through the day, which keeps gangways, staging rigged from the quay and access around a vessel lying alongside predictable for the whole shift.

port.h: Egersund harbour, Eigerøya and the pelagic fleet
p: Egersund lies on the Dalane coast of southern Rogaland, where the island of Eigerøya shelters a narrow sound from the North Sea and forms one of the finest natural harbours in Norway. Vessels reach the town's quays, fish factories and industrial waterfront through that protected water, without the long fjord passage many Norwegian ports demand. Because the coast outside faces the open North Sea, the harbour has long been used for shelter as well as for work, and its position close to the fishing grounds of the North Sea and the Skagerrak made it the country's leading landing port for many years, until Ålesund overtook it in the mid-2000s. The tidal range is negligible because the harbour lies close to an amphidromic point, so berthing, gangways and quay-side access are governed by weather rather than by the clock.

Fishing defines the port. Large pelagic purse seiners and trawlers bring catches of herring, mackerel, horse mackerel and blue whiting to the processing plants, where the fish is graded, frozen and stored before export. Landings follow the seasons of the different stocks, with autumn mackerel fishing among the busiest periods, and between seasons many vessels lie idle at the quays or go to a yard for maintenance. Alongside the fishing trade, the offshore fabrication yard at Egersund builds modules, topsides and subsea structures for the Norwegian shelf, which brings transport barges, heavy-lift ships, tugs and support vessels into the harbour whenever a structure is ready to leave. Frozen fish is shipped out in reefer ships and refrigerated containers, and coastal cargo ships bring in general cargo and supplies for the town and its industry.

For thickness gauging, Egersund offers long windows rather than short calls. A pelagic vessel between seasons may lie at the quay for weeks with its refrigerated sea-water (RSW) tanks pumped out and cleaned, and that is the obvious time to measure tanks, hull plating and the heavily loaded structure around winches, power blocks and trawl gallows. Barges and heavy-lift ships wait at the yard quay while load-out preparations run, often for several days. Reefer ships load frozen cargo over a day or two. The harbour is sheltered and the tide does not interfere, so the real limits are North Sea weather on open decks in winter and the fishing calendar itself: owners like to finish repairs before a season opens, so gauging needs booking early enough for any steel work to follow.

facilities.h: Quays, yard berths and lay-by space in Egersund
p: Fishing vessels are gauged alongside at the fish-factory quays or at lay-by berths in the harbour, once the crew or a shore contractor has cleaned and ventilated the tanks to be entered. RSW tanks must be pumped dry, washed and certified safe, because decomposing fish residues can release hydrogen sulphide and use up oxygen; the enclosed-space entry permit is issued by the vessel before anyone goes in, and the atmosphere is tested again during the work. Reefer ships at the processing plants' quays can have ballast tanks, deck plating and hatch coamings measured during loading, provided the team stays out of the way of the cargo flow.

At the fabrication yard, barges and heavy-lift ships lie at the load-out quay while sea fastening, ballasting and lifting are prepared, and measurement is fitted around the yard's programme and its permit system. Pelagic vessels usually dock at the specialist fishing-vessel yards further up the west coast, while barges and heavy-lift ships dock wherever their owners hold contracts. Readings taken in Egersund give those yards a realistic steel list before the vessel arrives, which shortens the time in dock and avoids surprises once the hull is dry.
list: Fish-factory quays — RSW tank, hull and fish-handling structure gauging on pelagic vessels between landings or seasons.
Lay-by berths in the harbour — longer condition surveys on fishing vessels laid up between seasons, with time to clean and open tanks in sequence.
Fabrication-yard load-out quay — deck plating, internal framing and ballast tank readings on transport barges and heavy-lift ships before loading.
Processing-plant quays used for reefer loading — ballast tank, deck and coaming measurements on reefer ships while frozen cargo goes aboard.
Harbour quays used by coastal cargo ships and tugs — targeted gauging after a survey finding or ahead of a docking.

context.h: Fishing-vessel rules, port state control and offshore logistics
p: Egersund's fishing fleet is largely Norwegian-flagged, and its vessels are surveyed under the Norwegian Maritime Authority's regulations for fishing vessels, with many of the larger ones also held in class. Thickness gauging on these ships is usually driven by class renewal surveys, by an owner preparing a vessel for sale or by the owner's own maintenance planning, rather than by the ESP rules that govern tankers and bulk carriers. Foreign-flagged reefers, cargo ships and heavy-lift vessels calling here fall under Paris MoU port state control, which the Norwegian Maritime Authority carries out, and an inspection finding on a wasted hatch coaming or air pipe can lead to a request for readings before departure.

Pelagic vessels wear in ways that cargo ships do not. RSW systems circulate chilled seawater through tanks and piping at high flow, and the mix of low temperature, oxygenated water, fish residues and repeated washing breaks down coatings and then the steel beneath. Pump sumps, suction wells, tank bottoms and the lower strakes of tank bulkheads are typical places for pitting. On deck, winch foundations, net-drum supports and gallows carry heavy cyclic loads that can crack welds long before wastage becomes a concern, so magnetic particle testing often goes with the gauging. For barges carrying modules from the yard, attention falls on the deck structure under the grillage and around the sea-fastening points.

jobs.h: What we typically gauge in Egersund
jobs.p: Most Egersund work is booked around the fishing calendar or the yard's load-out dates, both known well in advance, which suits a team that travels from India. Owners of pelagic vessels often want a full tank and hull picture before deciding what to repair at the next docking; barge operators want documented deck condition before a heavy cargo goes aboard. We agree the scope, the tank cleaning and the entry arrangements with the owner beforehand, then measure and send results each day so the steel list can be built as the work proceeds and the yard can be briefed before the vessel sails. Recurring requests include:
list: RSW tank gauging on a pelagic trawler laid up between seasons, with pitting at tank bottoms and suction wells mapped for repair.
Hull and bottom plating readings taken from inside a purse seiner, ahead of a docking at a west-coast fishing-vessel yard.
Magnetic particle testing of winch, net-drum and gallows foundations on a pelagic vessel, combined with deck plating gauging.
Deck plating, transverse framing and ballast tank gauging on a transport barge at the load-out quay before a module is moved aboard.
Tank-top, crane pedestal and deck measurements on a heavy-lift ship preparing to carry a structure from the fabrication yard.

logistics: Stavanger Airport, Sola, is the nearest international gateway; from there the team continues south by road or on the Jæren line commuter train, which ends at Egersund. Access to the fish-factory quays is arranged with the vessel owner and the plant, and the fabrication yard requires its own site induction and work permits, organised through the yard or the barge operator. Norway is a Schengen state, so each technician travels from India on a Schengen visa; season and load-out dates are usually known early, which leaves time for the application.

faqs.q: Can RSW tanks be gauged while a pelagic vessel is in season?
faqs.a: Only during a pause long enough to pump out, wash and ventilate the tanks, which a vessel in the middle of a season rarely has. In practice, RSW tank gauging is done between seasons or before a docking. If a crack or leak is suspected mid-season, a targeted check of a single tank can sometimes be fitted into a landing stop at Egersund, provided the tank is certified safe for entry.

faqs.q: Is thickness measurement on a fishing vessel different from a cargo ship?
faqs.a: The method is the same, but the structure and the scope differ. Fishing vessels are not covered by the ESP rules, so the gauging extent comes from the class rules for the vessel and its age, or from the owner's maintenance plan. The areas that matter most are the refrigerated tanks, the bottom and lower side plating, the stern and the foundations of the fishing gear, rather than cargo holds or topside tanks.

faqs.q: Can you gauge a barge for the marine warranty surveyor before load-out?
faqs.a: We can measure the barge and report the readings so that the owner can present them to the marine warranty surveyor, who decides what evidence the voyage needs. The usual scope is deck plating under the cargo footprint, the deck stiffeners and transverse frames below, ballast tanks and the towing bracket area, with magnetic particle testing at bracket and padeye welds where requested.

faqs.q: Where do Egersund fishing vessels go for dry-docking?
faqs.a: Usually to the fishing-vessel yards along the west coast where the owner holds a docking contract. Gauging in Egersund before the vessel leaves gives the yard a steel list in advance, so repairs can be planned and the docking kept no longer than necessary. If the owner prefers, the team can also travel on to the yard and complete the measurements while the hull is dry.

faqs.q: Does the tide affect access to vessels in Egersund?
faqs.a: Hardly at all. The harbour lies near an amphidromic point, so the water level changes very little over a day, and gangways and staging rigged from the quay stay usable throughout. Weather is the bigger factor: work on open decks and gear foundations is planned around North Sea wind and rain, while tank and engine-room work can continue in most conditions.
